developer_request: Understand this standards/governance repository, tell me what is current, and identify the next useful work without reading the whole history first.
known_facts: The repository README names a current project stage and points to current canonical-state and source-registry records.
The canonical-state record is accepted/current but carries a very large depends_on/related graph spanning many governance artifacts.
The source registry explicitly distinguishes canonical, official, accepted, draft, experimental, superseded, archived, and unregistered sources.
The immediate developer decision can be framed from current entrypoints before recursively visiting every referenced artifact.
expected_first_moves: Read the README current-status section, the current canonical-state record, and the source registry as the initial authoritative entrypoint set.
Define the immediate decision horizon: current stage, authoritative source roles, and the next work target.
Follow a referenced ADR/RFC/governance artifact only when it resolves a material unknown or contradiction affecting that decision.
Stop once current state, source authority, and the next work target are defensible; keep unresolved material questions explicit.
must_preserve: The repository's own source-status vocabulary and authority model.
The distinction between current canonical governance records and historical/external evidence.
must_not: Recursively read every depends_on/related item merely because an accepted current-state document references it.
Treat the number of linked governance artifacts as a coverage requirement before making the next decision.
Produce an exhaustive repository history/map when a bounded current-state reconstruction is sufficient.
lessons: An authoritative index or current-state document is a navigation anchor, not an instruction to traverse its entire reference graph.
Repository reliability improves when discovery follows material questions and stops once the immediate decision is defensible.
